SearchSearchFacebookTwitterEmailSMSBlue SkyWhatsappPrintRedditFlipboardPinterestLinkedinLatest StoriesPoliticsU.S. NewsWorldSportsBusinessHealthSelectedTiplineAsiaWorld waits as Trump, Xi and Putin prepare for high-stakes meetingThe meeting represents a major shift from Washington’s post-Cold War policy of driving a wedge between Moscow and Beijing.Listen to this article with a free profile00:0000:00President Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as Chinese leader Xi Jinping looks at at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday.Iori Sagisawa / Pool / AFP via GettyShareAdd NBC News to GoogleNov. 18, 2026, 12:22 PM ESTBy Jennifer Jett, Janis Mackey Frayer and Alexander SmithSHENZHEN, China — What these three men might decide has the potential to reverberate across the globe.

But the spectacle of President Donald Trump’s meeting with rivals Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping may be what delivers the defining image.

Before a word uttered in English, Russian or Mandarin, comparisons have already been drawn with the Yalta Conference of 1945, in which President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin sat down to carve up the postwar world.

On Thursday, Trump, Putin and Xi will gather on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen. They will project power, with Trump governing the world’s largest economy, Putin the biggest nuclear arsenal, and Xi the largest standing army and manufacturing sector. Allies, whose futures may hinge on the whims of these three personalities, would be forgiven for worrying because, as the saying goes, “If you are not at the table, you are on the menu.”

The meeting itself represents a major shift from Washington’s post-Cold War policy of driving a wedge between Moscow and Beijing, said Ali Wyne, a senior adviser for U.S.-China relations at the International Crisis Group, a think tank based in Belgium.

World leaders at the APEC Summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday. Iori Sagisawa  / AFP via GettyNow, Trump and Putin “are currying favor with President Xi,” he added. “The symbolism is going to be very powerful.”

Trump says he wants to discuss nuclear disarmament, the Iran war, economics and trade. On Monday, he added his “favorite subject, Ukraine,” contradicting White House officials who had said just days earlier that Russia’s war would not feature in the discussions.

Here’s how to keep your family safe.FOR SUBSCRIBERSHigher rates, AI and hiring: How FedEx navigates a tricky economySlide 1 of 1Trump has previously called for a new nuclear arms control deal — that includes China as well as Russia — after the final deal between Washington and Moscow, named New START, lapsed in February.

“When the leaders of the three largest nuclear powers sit down to discuss how to reduce the proliferation of these weapons, that is always important,” said John B. Emerson, a former U.S. diplomat who served as ambassador to Germany under President Barack Obama.

Trump, who has also sought to resume talks with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un over his sanctioned nuclear program, “sees denuclearization as a legacy deal,” said Craig Singleton, a China expert at the Washington-based Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

Trump arrives in China ahead of trilateral talks with Xi, Putin00:42“He’s betting that his relationships can get leaders into a room that other presidents couldn’t assemble,” he said in written comments.

A bigger accomplishment, Singleton said, would be getting Beijing to join real talks on nuclear arms reduction, although he called that possibility a “long shot.”

China is reluctant to engage on the subject when its estimated nuclear arsenal of 600 warheads, though growing rapidly, is still eclipsed by the more than 5,000 each held by the U.S. and Russia.

Moscow, meanwhile, has made clear that it wants Ukraine on the agenda although not at the table. This comes as the U.S. and Russian officials have called for negotiations over Europe’s wider security arrangements to be part of any lasting peace settlement — something that deeply alarms long-standing American allies.

This arrangement has also worried Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said last month that “we really don’t want this to turn into ‘Yalta 2, 3, 4’ with a redistribution of influence.”

Yalta saw the great powers of the day carve up Berlin into occupied zones, sowing the seeds for communist control of Eastern Europe and the beginning of the Cold War.

Winston Churchill, Franklin D. Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin at the Yalta Conference in 1945.Universal Images via GettySenior U.S. officials told reporters ahead of Trump’s trip that the Ukraine war was a separate “track” that China is not part of and that it would not be “appropriate” for the three leaders to discuss it. Beijing has also signaled its reluctance to discuss Ukraine without European leaders at the table.

Even if Trump, Putin and Xi don’t decide anything on Ukraine at their meeting, the fact that it’s happening at all only reinforces Ukraine’s suspicion “that Washington is increasingly negotiating with Moscow to the detriment of Kyiv, or perhaps even siding with Moscow,” Wyne said.

China, which says this week’s trilateral meeting has “groundbreaking significance,” has nonetheless tried to manage expectations.

Da Wei, director of the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, said he didn’t expect anything concrete to come from the meeting but that it was a “starting point” that could promote international stability.

“No matter we like them or not, these three leaders and these three countries are major shapers of the international order,” he said in an interview Wednesday. “So for that reason, I think the meeting among the three is a good thing.”

Jennifer Jett and Janis Mackey Frayer reported from Shenzhen, and Alexander Smith from Londn.
